prompt: Ana runs `git rm --cached terraform.tfvars`, adds `*.tfvars` to `.gitignore` and commits. Who can still read the password she had committed weeks before?
hint: `git show HEAD~1:terraform.tfvars` answered.

choices.text: Whoever has a clone of the repository
choices.why: Yes. The new commit stops tracking the file; the old commit still holds it, in every clone, fork and backup.

choices.text: Nobody, since the file has left the repository
choices.why: It left the next commit. The capture printed it from the one before.

choices.text: People who check out the newest commit
choices.why: The newest commit is precisely the one without the file.

choices.text: Whoever can read the state bucket
choices.why: The state is a different copy, and there was no apply yet. The question is about git.

prompt: A password was committed and pushed to the shop's repository a month ago. What is the repair the lesson says works?
hint: Think about the clones you do not control.

choices.text: Rewrite the history and force-push the result
choices.why: That cleans this copy of the repository and reaches none of the clones already made.

choices.text: Mark the variable `sensitive = true`
choices.why: That changes what Terraform prints, not what git stored a month ago.

choices.text: Rotate it
choices.why: Yes. Change the password at the database and treat the old one as public, because it is.

choices.text: Add `*.tfvars` to `.gitignore` and commit again
choices.why: Right for the future, and it does nothing for the commit that already carries the file.

prompt: Before any apply, where did the lesson find the password Ana wrote in `terraform.tfvars`? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three copies come before the state exists.

choices.text: In the git history
choices.why: Yes, in the commit that carried the file.

choices.text: In the plan printed on the screen
choices.why: Yes, inside `user_data`, before it was marked sensitive.

choices.text: In `.terraform.lock.hcl`
choices.why: The lock file records provider versions and hashes, no values.

choices.text: Inside the saved plan file `tfplan`
choices.why: Yes: `grep` found it on two lines of the unzipped archive.

choices.text: In the attributes of the AMI data source
choices.why: The image lookup has nothing to do with the password.

prompt: Once a password has been committed and pushed, the repair that works is to ___ it: set a new one at the database and treat the old value as public.
hint: The word for replacing a secret on purpose.

prompt: What does `sensitive = true` on a variable change?
hint: The section calls it a promise about one thing.

choices.text: The state stores that value encrypted
choices.why: The capture found the password in the state in plain text after the marking.

choices.text: What Terraform prints
choices.why: Yes. It hides the value in plans and listings, and changes nothing on disk.

choices.text: The value is left out of a saved plan file
choices.why: A saved plan carries the values it was made with, marked or not.

choices.text: Outputs refuse to return it, even with `-raw`
choices.why: `terraform output -raw db_password` printed it.

prompt: With the variable marked sensitive, why does Terraform refuse `output "db_password" { value = var.db_password }`?
hint: Read the last line of the error.

choices.text: A root module may not export a password at all
choices.why: It may; the next attempt, with one more argument, applied.

choices.text: Outputs cannot refer to input variables
choices.why: They can; the corrected output still says `var.db_password`.

choices.text: The output has to be marked sensitive itself
choices.why: Yes. A value built from a secret has to say so where it leaves the configuration.

choices.text: The variable has no default
choices.why: The value came from `terraform.tfvars`; a default has nothing to do with it.

prompt: `terraform output` lists `db_password = <sensitive>`. Which of these commands prints the password itself?
hint: An output exists to be read by something.

choices.text: `terraform plan`
choices.why: The plan shows `(sensitive value)` in its place.

choices.text: `terraform output -json`
choices.why: Yes. Asked for by name or as JSON, a sensitive output hands over its value.

choices.text: `terraform show`
choices.why: `show` renders the state the way the plan renders a change, with sensitive values hidden.

choices.text: `terraform output` with `TF_LOG=debug` set
choices.why: A debug log adds Terraform's own messages; the listing still says `<sensitive>`.

prompt: After the variable and the output were both marked sensitive and applied, on how many lines of `terraform.tfstate` did `grep -c` find the password?
hint: One for the output, one for the script that writes the file.

prompt: Nobody typed the password `random_password` generated. Where is it after the apply?
hint: `jq` printed two of them.

choices.text: In the state, in plain text
choices.why: Yes: as `result` and again as `secret_string`.

choices.text: Nowhere, because Terraform discards the values it generates
choices.why: It keeps them; that is how the next run knows the password already exists.

choices.text: In the state, as a bcrypt hash and no more
choices.why: The hash is there as well, beside the password itself.

choices.text: In Secrets Manager, and not on Ana's disk
choices.why: Secrets Manager has it, and so does the state on her disk.

prompt: Why does `random_password` keep its `result` in the state at all?
hint: What would the next plan do without it?

choices.text: Because the provider forgot to mark it sensitive
choices.why: It is marked: `sensitive_attributes` listed `result`.

choices.text: So that `terraform output` has something to print
choices.why: The configuration had no output at all.

choices.text: Because Secrets Manager reads the password back from the state
choices.why: AWS never reads Terraform's state; it got the value through the API.

choices.text: So the next run reuses it
choices.why: Yes. Without the stored value every plan would generate a new password.

prompt: Another team creates its passwords by hand in Secrets Manager and reads them into Terraform with `data "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version"`. What does their state hold?
hint: Ana's `read.tf` only read.

choices.text: The ARN of each secret and no value
choices.why: That is the managed arrangement of a later section, where Terraform never asks for the value.

choices.text: Nothing, since a data source is read-only
choices.why: Read-only describes AWS, not the state: what is read is recorded.

choices.text: Every password it reads, in plain text
choices.why: Yes. The data source's `secret_string` was the third copy in the section.

choices.text: Each password as a hash
choices.why: Nothing hashes a value read by a data source.

prompt: The state lists `result` under `sensitive_attributes` for `random_password`. What does Terraform use that list for?
hint: Compare what the plan showed with what `jq` found.

choices.text: To encrypt those attributes before writing
choices.why: `jq` read them in plain text right beside the list.

choices.text: To keep those values off the screen
choices.why: Yes. It knows which values are secret and hides them when printing, and writes them all the same.

choices.text: To skip them when comparing in a plan
choices.why: They are compared like any other attribute; that is why they are kept.

choices.text: To leave them out of `terraform state pull`
choices.why: A pull returns the state exactly as stored.

prompt: `secret_string = ephemeral.random_password.db.result` fails with `Invalid use of ephemeral value`. Why?
hint: The error says what `secret_string` is not.

choices.text: `random_password` exists only as a managed resource
choices.why: The random provider has the ephemeral form too; the error is about where the value goes.

choices.text: `secret_string` is persisted to the state
choices.why: Yes. An ephemeral value may only go somewhere nothing is written down, such as a write-only argument.

choices.text: The AWS provider in the lab accepts no ephemeral values
choices.why: It accepted one in `secret_string_wo` on the next try.

choices.text: Terraform 1.16 needs `ephemeral = true` on the resource
choices.why: There is no such argument on a resource; `ephemeral = true` belongs to variables and outputs.

prompt: An argument that accepts an ephemeral value, passes it to the provider during the apply and keeps no record of it is a ___ argument, and its name ends in `_wo`.
hint: Two words joined by a hyphen.

prompt: The ephemeral resource generated a new password on the second run, and `terraform plan` said `No changes`. Why?
hint: What is there in the state to compare?

choices.text: The ephemeral resource returns the same password every time
choices.why: It produces a fresh one whenever it is opened, which was twice in a single apply.

choices.text: AWS refused the second password
choices.why: Nothing was sent, so AWS had nothing to refuse.

choices.text: Terraform has no stored value to compare it with
choices.why: Yes. It only resends the value when `secret_string_wo_version` changes.

choices.text: The plan skipped the ephemeral resource
choices.why: Plans open it too; the apply transcript showed it opened while planning.

prompt: Put what happened during `terraform apply` with the write-only argument in order.
hint: The ephemeral resource is opened twice.
items: The ephemeral password is opened and closed to make the plan
The ephemeral password is opened again for the apply
The secret version is created with the value
The ephemeral password is closed and the value dropped
trap: Many expect a single opening. The plan needs the value too, so the resource is opened once for the plan and once for the apply.

prompt: With `manage_master_user_password = true`, what does the state hold about the database password?
hint: `password` was null.

choices.text: The password, marked sensitive
choices.why: `password` was null in the state; Terraform never received it.

choices.text: A bcrypt hash of it
choices.why: That was `random_password`'s extra attribute, not the database's.

choices.text: The ARN of the secret that holds it, with its KMS key
choices.why: Yes: `master_user_secret` names where the password is, not what it is.

choices.text: The password, encrypted with KMS
choices.why: The KMS key in the state is the one Secrets Manager uses; the password itself is not there.

prompt: In the managed arrangement, how does the shop's application get the database password?
hint: It is not Terraform's job any more.

choices.text: From a Terraform output read at deploy time
choices.why: The only output is the ARN, which says where the password is.

choices.text: It asks Secrets Manager, by ARN, when it starts
choices.why: Yes, with an IAM policy allowing `GetSecretValue` on that one secret.

choices.text: From a file `user_data` writes when the machine boots
choices.why: That was the leaking design of the first section.

choices.text: From the state, through `terraform_remote_state`
choices.why: The state does not hold the password, so there is nothing to read there.

prompt: What does letting RDS manage the password buy, according to the lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: Look back at the four copies, and at who rotates.

choices.text: The password is in none of the four copies
choices.why: Yes: not in git, a printed plan, a plan file or the state.

choices.text: A rotation needs no apply
choices.why: Yes; RDS and Secrets Manager rotate it between themselves.

choices.text: The application needs no change to its code
choices.why: The cost moves there: it has to fetch the secret and fetch it again after a rotation.

choices.text: Every read is an API call a real account logs
choices.why: Yes, in CloudTrail; moto keeps no such log, so the lab could not show it.

choices.text: Terraform notices when the password changes
choices.why: Terraform never sees the password, so it has nothing to notice.

prompt: Against whom does `encrypt = true` in the S3 backend protect the state?
hint: Where is the object encrypted, and who gets it decrypted?

choices.text: A colleague whose IAM policy lets them read the bucket
choices.why: S3 decrypts the object for every authorised reader.

choices.text: Somebody holding a copy from `terraform state pull`
choices.why: That copy left the bucket decrypted.

choices.text: Somebody reading S3's disks
choices.why: Yes. The object is encrypted at rest, and handed over in plain text to whoever the bucket lets in.

choices.text: A pipeline log that prints the plan
choices.why: A log is not the bucket at all; that is what `sensitive` is for.

prompt: In the OpenTofu configuration, what is the `fallback` with the `unencrypted` method for?
hint: It was removed right after one apply.

choices.text: Reading the state that was still plain
choices.why: Yes. Without it, OpenTofu would try to decrypt a file that was never encrypted.

choices.text: Writing a readable copy beside the encrypted state
choices.why: A fallback is about reading; `grep` found no `result` anywhere in the file.

choices.text: Letting Terraform read the encrypted state
choices.why: Terraform failed on the file: it does not know the format.

choices.text: Opening the state when the passphrase is lost
choices.why: Left in place it would accept a plain file, not decrypt an encrypted one.

prompt: Why is the passphrase a variable, set as `TF_VAR_state_passphrase`, and not written into `encryption.tf`?
hint: Where does `encryption.tf` end up?

choices.text: OpenTofu rejects a literal passphrase
choices.why: A literal would work; the problem is where the file goes.

choices.text: Because `encryption.tf` is committed with the rest of the configuration
choices.why: Yes. A passphrase in it would be one more secret in the git history.

choices.text: A variable makes the key longer
choices.why: The key length comes from the key provider (32 in `meta`), not from where the passphrase was written.

choices.text: To keep the passphrase out of the encrypted state
choices.why: The passphrase is never stored in the state; `meta` holds a salt and parameters.

prompt: A year after the migration, the passphrase is lost. The bucket is versioned. What in it can still be read?
hint: Which versions were never encrypted?

choices.text: Every version, by deriving the key from the salt in `meta`
choices.why: The salt is half of the derivation; the passphrase is the other half.

choices.text: The latest version, because S3 decrypts it for an authorised reader
choices.why: S3 removes its own encryption, not OpenTofu's.

choices.text: The versions from before the migration
choices.why: Yes, in plain text, which is why the lesson says to delete them and rotate what they held.

choices.text: Nothing, since S3 deletes the versions OpenTofu cannot read
choices.why: S3 knows nothing about OpenTofu's encryption and deletes nothing on its own.

prompt: Match each measure to the copy of the password it removes.
hint: Five measures, five places, one place left over.

pairs.right: The plan on a screen or in a CI log

pairs.left: A write-only argument fed by an ephemeral value
pairs.right: The state and the saved plan file
Every copy: Terraform never sees it
The plain text of a state that left the program

right_distractors: The value inside the running application

prompt: A colleague's configuration reads the shop's existing password with `data "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version"` and passes it to `password` on `aws_db_instance`. With the lab's AWS provider, which change keeps the password out of the state and still uses that secret?
hint: Two halves: how it is read, and where it goes.

choices.text: Mark the data source and the `password` argument sensitive
choices.why: That hides the value on the screen; both copies stay in the state.

choices.text: Read it with the ephemeral resource and pass it to `password_wo`
choices.why: Yes. Both exist in the lab's provider: the ephemeral form of the secret version, and `aws_db_instance` in the write-only list.

choices.text: Move the data source into a child module
choices.why: A child module's resources and data sources go into the same state.

choices.text: Add `password` to `lifecycle { ignore_changes }`
choices.why: `ignore_changes` changes what a plan compares, and the value is still stored.

prompt: Ana's team wants to encrypt the state of an existing configuration with OpenTofu. Put the steps in order.
hint: The fallback is there for exactly one run.
items: Store the passphrase in the pipeline's secret store as `TF_VAR_state_passphrase`
Add the `encryption` block with an `unencrypted` fallback
Run `tofu apply`, which writes the state encrypted
Remove the fallback and the `unencrypted` method
Delete the plain versions in the bucket and rotate what they held
trap: Removing the fallback before the first encrypted write leaves OpenTofu unable to read the plain state it starts from.

prompt: A reviewer reads a pull request: `random_password` feeds `secret_string`, and every variable and output is marked sensitive. The description says the password is now safe. What does the reviewer reply?
hint: Count the copies `jq` found.

choices.text: Approve: nothing generated by Terraform is stored
choices.why: `random_password` stores its result on purpose, so the next run reuses it.

choices.text: Approve, if the state bucket has `encrypt = true`
choices.why: That protects S3's disks; every reader of the bucket gets the state in plain text.

choices.text: The state holds it twice; use an ephemeral password and `secret_string_wo`
choices.why: Yes. `sensitive` only hides it on screen, and the write-only pair keeps it out of the state.

choices.text: Ask for `ignore_changes = [secret_string]`
choices.why: That stops later plans from updating it and still stores the value.
